questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'the database feels slow' is a symptom, not a diagnosis?
options: Because it could stem from three genuinely different resource constraints — CPU-bound, IO-bound, or memory-bound — each requiring a different fix, so scaling compute without identifying which one is exhausted may not help at all
Because slowness always means the database needs a full DBCC CHECKDB run
Because slowness is always caused by fragmented indexes specifically
Because Azure Monitor cannot measure database performance
questions.explain: Scaling compute throws capacity at the problem without confirming which resource is actually the bottleneck, which can leave the real cause unaddressed.

questions.q: What does a high signal_wait_time_ms relative to total wait time in sys.dm_os_wait_stats indicate?
options: Queries are ready to run and are simply waiting for a free CPU — a genuinely CPU-bound condition
The database has run out of disk storage
Statistics are stale and need to be updated
SQL Server Agent jobs have stopped running
questions.explain: High signal wait relative to resource wait specifically points to CPU contention — queries are runnable but there's no free core.

questions.q: Why can high PAGEIOLATCH waits or io_stall be a 'query problem wearing an IO-bound costume' rather than a real storage bottleneck?
options: Because a missing index can force full table scans that read far more data than necessary, generating heavy IO that no storage-tier upgrade would actually fix — the real fix is the index, not more IOPS
Because PAGEIOLATCH waits are always caused by network latency, never disk
Because io_stall values are randomly generated and mean nothing
Because IO-bound bottlenecks can only occur on Azure SQL Database, never elsewhere
questions.explain: The lesson's core distinction: a resource symptom can be caused by a real shortage, or by a query design problem that scaling doesn't address.

questions.q: What does a falling page life expectancy combined with high RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits typically indicate?
options: Memory pressure — either a genuine memory shortage for the working data set, or a query pattern reading far more data than necessary and forcing cache churn
The SQL Server Agent service account lacks the correct permissions
The database has corruption requiring DBCC CHECKDB with REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS
Statistics have not been updated in over 30 days
questions.explain: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits are queries waiting on memory grants, and falling page life expectancy shows pages being evicted faster than expected — both point to memory pressure, real or query-induced.

questions.q: What does Chapter 9 close out, and what does Chapter 10 do next, per this lesson?
options: Chapter 9 covered database maintenance and configuration (index/statistics maintenance, integrity checks, scoped configuration, Resource Governor, and bottleneck diagnosis); Chapter 10 automates this routine work with SQL Server Agent
Chapter 9 covered backup and restore; Chapter 10 covers high availability and disaster recovery
Chapter 9 covered SQL Server Agent; Chapter 10 covers query performance tuning
Chapter 9 and Chapter 10 cover identical material in a different order
questions.explain: Chapter 10, SQL Server Agent & Automation, picks up right where Chapter 9 leaves off — automating the maintenance work covered here.
